item.title: Privacy Policy
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Who we are

Suggested text: Our website address is: https://dexmetal.com.

Comments

Suggested text: When visitors leave comments on the site we collect the data shown in the comments form, and also the visitor’s IP address and browser user agent string to help spam detection.

An anonymized string created from your email address (also called a hash) may be provided to the Gravatar service to see if you are using it. The Gravatar service privacy policy is available here: https://automattic.com/privacy/. After approval of your comment, your profile picture is visible to the public in the context of your comment.

Media

Suggested text: If you upload images to the website, you should avoid uploading images with embedded location data (EXIF GPS) included. Visitors to the website can download and extract any location data from images on the website.

Cookies

Suggested text: If you leave a comment on our site you may opt-in to saving your name, email address and website in cookies. These are for your convenience so that you do not have to fill in your details again when you leave another comment. These cookies will last for one year.

If you visit our login page, we will set a temporary cookie to determine if your browser accepts cookies. This cookie contains no personal data and is discarded when you close your browser.

When you log in, we will also set up several cookies to save your login information and your screen display choices. Login cookies last for two days, and screen options cookies last for a year. If you select "Remember Me", your login will persist for two weeks. If you log out of your account, the login cookies will be removed.

If you edit or publish an article, an additional cookie will be saved in your browser. This cookie includes no personal data and simply indicates the post ID of the article you just edited. It expires after 1 day.

Embedded content from other websites

Suggested text: Articles on this site may include embedded content (e.g. videos, images, articles, etc.). Embedded content from other websites behaves in the exact same way as if the visitor has visited the other website.

These websites may collect data about you, use cookies, embed additional third-party tracking, and monitor your interaction with that embedded content, including tracking your interaction with the embedded content if you have an account and are logged in to that website.

Who we share your data with

Suggested text: If you request a password reset, your IP address will be included in the reset email.

How long we retain your data

Suggested text: If you leave a comment, the comment and its metadata are retained indefinitely. This is so we can recognize and approve any follow-up comments automatically instead of holding them in a moderation queue.

For users that register on our website (if any), we also store the personal information they provide in their user profile. All users can see, edit, or delete their personal information at any time (except they cannot change their username). Website administrators can also see and edit that information.

What rights you have over your data

Suggested text: If you have an account on this site, or have left comments, you can request to receive an exported file of the personal data we hold about you, including any data you have provided to us. You can also request that we erase any personal data we hold about you. This does not include any data we are obliged to keep for administrative, legal, or security purposes.

Where your data is sent

Suggested text: Visitor comments may be checked through an automated spam detection service.

item.title: Basel Export Application Form Guide (Notification Document)
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
← Back to Basel Knowledge Hub

Blocks 1–10: Party and Waste Identification

Block 1

Exporter-Notifier Registration

Identifies the legal entity initiating the transboundary movement. Competent authorities use this block to verify the notifier's registration status, country of origin, and legal authority to export hazardous waste under the Basel Convention.

View guide →
Block 2

Importer-Consignee Information

Names the receiving facility and the country of import. This block establishes the destination party's legal identity and must match the consignee named in any pre-consented or bilateral agreement between the countries concerned.

View guide →
Block 3

Notification Number & Shipment Type

Records the unique reference number assigned by the competent authority upon notification submission. Also specifies whether the movement is a single shipment or part of a general notification covering multiple trips.

View guide →
Block 4

Total Intended Number of Shipments

Declares the total number of individual trips planned under a general notification. Competent authorities use this figure when evaluating the scale of the movement and assessing environmental risk exposure over the consent period.

View guide →
Block 5

Total Intended Quantity

States the total weight or volume of hazardous waste covered by the notification in metric tonnes or litres. Discrepancies between notified and actual quantities are a leading cause of customs holds and compliance violations.

View guide →
Block 6

Intended Period of Time for Shipment(s)

Defines the start and end dates during which shipments may legally move under the consent. Movements outside the approved period are treated as unauthorised transboundary movements under Basel Article 9.

View guide →
Block 7

Packaging Type(s) & Special Handling

Specifies the UN-approved packaging codes and flags special handling requirements. Incorrect packaging declarations are among the most common causes of notification rejection by importing country authorities.

View guide →
Block 8

Intended Carrier(s)

Lists all carriers authorised to transport the waste, including registration numbers and countries. Adding an unlisted carrier during transit requires a formal amendment to the notification before movement begins.

View guide →
Block 9

Waste Generator-Producer

Identifies the original producer of the hazardous waste. This block creates the legal chain of custody from waste origin through export and is referenced in enforcement proceedings.

View guide →
Block 10

Disposal/Recovery Facility

Names the licensed facility performing final treatment, disposal, or recovery in the country of import. The facility must hold valid operating permits under the importing country's domestic law at the time consent is granted.

View guide →

Blocks 11–21: Technical and Administrative Details

Block 11

Disposal/Recovery Operation

Records the Basel Convention Annex IV operation code (D or R code) describing how the waste will be processed. Selecting the wrong code is a common error that triggers requests for additional information from importing authorities.

View guide →
Block 12

Designation & Composition of the Waste

Provides the physical and chemical composition of the hazardous waste in plain language. Authorities rely on this block to confirm the waste matches the hazard codes declared elsewhere in the form.

View guide →
Block 13

Waste Physical Characteristics

Describes the physical state of the waste — solid, liquid, sludge, gaseous, or other. This directly affects packaging requirements, transport regulations, and the environmental risk assessment during consent review.

View guide →
Block 14

Waste Identification and Classification

The most technically complex block. Lists applicable Basel Annex codes, OECD codes, national codes, and UN hazard classes. Classification errors here account for the majority of notification rejections across all Basel Party states.

View guide →
Block 15

Countries/States Concerned & Border Crossings

Maps the complete transit route from country of export to country of import. Each transit country listed has the right to grant or withhold consent under Article 6 of the Basel Convention.

View guide →
Block 16

Customs Offices (EU Member States Only)

Required only for shipments entering or exiting EU member states under Regulation (EC) No 1013/2006. Non-EU movements leave this block blank but must not omit it from the form.

View guide →
Block 17

Exporter & Generator Declaration

The legally binding signature block where the exporter and generator certify the accuracy of all information. An unsigned or undated Block 17 renders the entire notification invalid.

View guide →
Block 18

Number of Annexes Attached

Declares how many supporting annexes accompany the notification. The number stated must exactly match the physical documents submitted — missing annexes are the most common reason a notification is declared incomplete on first review.

View guide →
Block 19

Competent Authority Acknowledgement

Completed by the importing country's competent authority to confirm receipt. Under Article 13, acknowledgement must be issued within three working days. The financial guarantee typically cannot be released until this block is returned.

View guide →
Block 20

Competent Authority Consent/Objection

Records formal written consent or objection from all competent authorities concerned. No physical shipment may begin until all required consents are in hand and no valid objection is outstanding.

View guide →
Block 21

Specific Conditions or Objection Reasons

Used by competent authorities to attach legally binding conditions to a consent or to state formal reasons for objection. All conditions must be met before and during each individual shipment.

View guide →

wp:postmeta.wp:meta_value: Field-by-field guidance for every Basel Convention notification document block. Understand exactly what each field requires for hazardous waste export compliance.

item.title: Block 1: Exporter-Notifier Registration
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 1: Exporter-Notifier Registration

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 1

Block 1 – Quick Reference

Exporter-Notifier Registration

Identifies the legally accountable notifier responsible for initiating and managing the transboundary movement.

Basel Basis
vCOP8 Section IV
ID Type
Exporter registration number
Required For
All Basel notifications

What Block 1 Captures

The Exporter-Notifier Registration block is the regulatory anchor of any Basel notification. It identifies the legal entity responsible for the accuracy of the filing and compliance of the movement.

This entity remains legally accountable for the waste from origin until formal acceptance by the disposal or recovery facility. Under vCOP8 guidance, the notifier may be the waste generator, a recognized trader, or a competent authority of the State of export.

How to Complete Block 1

1
Enter the full legal entity name. Match official business registration records exactly.
2
Add the valid registration number. Use the currently active identifier issued in the State of export.
3
Provide the registered physical address. Use headquarters or legal address, not warehouse or logistics addresses.
4
Include direct contact details. Add phone, fax, email, and a designated contact person authorized to manage the notification.
⚠️
Notifier Identity Must Match Registration

Do not list a dispatch warehouse, broker, or logistics provider as the notifier unless they hold legal standing. Block 1 must reflect the registered entity that is legally liable for the movement.

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
Using dispatch center address
Correct
Use legal registered headquarters address
Wrong
Listing logistics provider as notifier
Correct
List only entity with legal notifier authority
Wrong
Using outdated registration details
Correct
Use current registration matching valid license

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a freight forwarder be listed as the notifier?▼

Only if the forwarder has formal legal standing and assumes notifier obligations. Otherwise, list the registered exporter entity.

If exporter and generator are the same, what should Block 9 show?▼

Block 9 may indicate “Same as Block 1” where allowed by vCOP8 instructions and local authority practice.

Are PO boxes acceptable for Block 1?▼

No. Use a complete physical address tied to the legally registered notifier entity.

Supporting Documents

  • Doc 1: Exporter Registration Certificate - Model legal framework for permits, licenses and compliance controls.
  • Doc 18: Notification Summary Sheet (Annex V-A) - Official Annex V-A/V-B forms and completion instructions.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

For ULAB and e-waste exports, confirm the notifier registration number matches the current environmental license. Expired or mismatched registrations are a leading cause of shipment holds.

← Back toBasel Form GuideNext →Block 2: Importer-Consignee Information

Need Help Completing Your Notification?

DexMetal’s Basel compliance tools guide you through every block with validation and country-specific guidance.

Explore the Knowledge Hub →

item.title: Block 2: Importer-Consignee Information
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 2: Importer-Consignee Information

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 2

Block 2 — Quick Reference

Importer-Consignee Information

Identifies the legal entity responsible for waste upon entry into the country of import.

Basel Article
Annex VII
ID Type
Legal entity identifier
Required For
All import notifications

What Block 2 Captures

Block 2 identifies the Importer-Consignee — the entity legally responsible for the waste once it enters the jurisdiction of the country of import.

This party is often the same as the disposal or recovery facility listed in Block 10, but as specified in vCOP8 (Section IV, Paragraph 15), the importer may also be a recognized trader, broker, or corporate headquarters. The primary requirement is that the importer must be under the jurisdiction of the country of import and maintain direct legal control over the waste at the moment of arrival.

How to Complete Block 2

1
Confirm importer jurisdiction. Verify the importer is legally registered in the country of import.
2
Enter full legal entity name. Match official regulatory filings exactly — no abbreviations unless on the license.
3
Verify facility address. Provide the primary place of business or processing location — not a P.O. Box.
4
Include direct contact details. Add verified phone, fax, and named contact person for customs communication.
⚠️
Importer Must Be Legally Registered

The importer must be legally registered in the country of import — not just the final destination facility. A facility address and importer legal identity are not always the same, and mismatches cause notifications to be returned by the competent authority.

Common Errors → Correct Approach

❌ Wrong
Listing a broker without legal “possession or control”
✅ Correct
Broker must assume full liability under vCOP8
❌ Wrong
Using headquarters address when subsidiary is the importer
✅ Correct
Use the local subsidiary’s registered address
❌ Wrong
Providing a P.O. Box as the facility address
✅ Correct
Physical address of the processing or storage facility

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a broker be listed as importer?▼

Yes, but only if the broker has legal “possession or control” of the waste and assumes full liability under vCOP8. The broker must be registered in the country of import.

What if the importer and disposal facility are different?▼

This is common. Block 2 identifies the importer while Block 10 identifies the disposal/recovery facility. Both must be legally registered in their respective jurisdictions.

Is a P.O. Box acceptable?▼

No. The address must denote the primary place of business or the specific location where the waste will be initially processed or stored. P.O. Boxes are not acceptable.

Supporting Documents

  • Doc 2: Consignee Import License - Model legal framework for permits, licenses and compliance controls.
  • Doc 18.1: National Notification Form (NZ example) - Reference document for this block requirement.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

For ULAB imports into developing markets, verify the importer holds a valid waste import license separate from standard business registration. Many jurisdictions require a separate environmental import permit.

← Back toBlock 1: Exporter-NotifierNext →Block 3: Notification Number System

Explore the Knowledge Hub →

item.title: TEST
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
What You'll Find Here

The Basel Movement Document (Annex V-B), often called the "Passport," must accompany the hazardous waste shipment at all times from the moment it leaves the exporter's facility until it reaches the disposal site. This guide breaks down the 19 numbered blocks required to maintain a legal chain of custody and avoid illegal traffic penalties.

Crucial Rule: Information in this document must strictly match the details in your authorized Notification Document.

Movement Document Block Index

Part 1: Shipment Identification (Before Departure)

  • Block 1: Notification Number
  • Block 2: Serial/Total Number of Shipments
  • Block 3: Exporter - Notifier
  • Block 4: Importer - Consignee
  • Block 5: Actual Quantity (Weight/Volume)
  • Block 6: Actual Date of Shipment
  • Block 7: Packaging & Handling

Part 2: Chain of Custody (During Transport)

  • Block 8(a-c): Carrier Transfer Signatures
  • Block 9: Waste Generator
  • Block 15: Exporter's Declaration (Signature)
  • Block 16: Customs Offices (Entry/Exit)

Part 3: Waste Details & Identification

  • Blocks 10-11: Disposal/Recovery Facility
  • Block 12: Designation of Waste
  • Block 13: Physical Characteristics
  • Block 14: Waste Identification Codes

Part 4: Arrival & Disposal Confirmation

  • Block 17: Importer Acceptance
  • Block 18: Receipt at Facility
  • Block 19: Certification of Disposal/Recovery

Detailed Block Instructions

Block 1: Notification Number

What goes here: The unique ID of your approved Notification Document.

Instruction: Copy this exactly from Block 3 of your Notification form. It links this specific truckload to your government permission.

Block 2: Serial/Total Number of Shipments

What goes here: Tracking the count of shipments against your total limit.

Instruction: If your Notification authorized 10 total shipments, and this is the 3rd one, write: 3 / 10. If this is a single shipment notification, write 1 / 1.

Blocks 3 & 4: Exporter and Importer

What goes here: The legal entities trading the waste.

Instruction: Reproduce the exact same information (Name, Address, Contact) as found in Blocks 1 and 2 of the Notification Document. Do not change company names here.

Block 5: Actual Quantity

What goes here: The specific weight of the cargo on this specific vehicle.

Instruction: Enter the Actual Weight (Tonnes/Mg) or Volume. Pro Tip: Attach the Weighbridge Ticket to this document as proof. Do not enter the "Total Estimated Quantity" from the Notification.

Block 6: Actual Date of Shipment

What goes here: The date the truck physically leaves the Exporter's facility.

Compliance Check: This date must fall within the "Validity Period" listed on the Written Consent letters from the Competent Authorities.

Block 7: Packaging & Handling

What goes here: How the waste is packed.

Instruction: Use standard codes (e.g., 1 for Drum, 5 for Bag). Indicate the number of packages. If special handling is required (e.g., "Keep Dry"), check "Yes" and attach instructions.

Block 8 (a-c): Carrier Transfer Signatures

What goes here: The Chain of Custody.

Instruction: Every person who drives/transports the waste must sign here.

  • 8(a): 1st Carrier (Pick up driver). Signs at moment of pick up.
  • 8(b): 2nd Carrier (e.g., Shipping Line or Rail).
  • 8(c): Last Carrier (Delivery driver).

Block 9: Waste Generator

Instruction: Copy the Generator details from Block 9 of the Notification Document.

Blocks 10 & 11: Disposal/Recovery Facility

Instruction: Copy the Facility details and Operation Code (e.g., R4, D5) from Blocks 10 and 11 of the Notification Document. The technology employed must match.

Blocks 12, 13, 14: Waste Identification

Instruction: These blocks must be identical to the Notification Document.

  • Block 12: Name of the waste.
  • Block 13: Physical characteristics (e.g., Powder, Solid).
  • Block 14: Basel Code (e.g., A1180), OECD Code, UN Number, etc.

Block 15: Exporter's Declaration

Action: The Exporter (or authorized broker) must sign and date here before the shipment leaves.

Legal Meaning: By signing, you certify the information is true, insurance is valid, and contracts are legally binding.

Block 16: Customs Offices

Instruction: Only required if national legislation of the Export/Transit/Import country demands it. Customs officers will stamp 'Exit', 'Entry', or 'Export' here.

Block 17: Importer Acceptance

Action: The Importer signs here immediately upon the waste arriving in the destination country. (Note: If Importer = Disposer, proceed to Block 18).

Block 18: Receipt at Facility

Action: The Disposal/Recovery Facility signs here immediately upon the truck arriving at the gate.

Crucial Step: They must check "Accepted" or "Rejected". If rejected, authorities must be contacted immediately.

Block 19: Certification of Disposal/Recovery

The Final Step: The Facility signs this block only after the recycling/disposal work is 100% complete.

Instruction: This must be done within 30 days of completion. The Facility must send signed copies to the Exporter and the Competent Authorities. This is required to release your financial bond.

Back to Top

item.title: Block 13: Physical Characteristics
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 13: Physical Characteristics

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Movement Guide / Block 13

Block 13 – Quick Reference

Physical Characteristics

Identifies the physical state of the waste at normal temperature and pressure using standardized codes.

Basel Basis
Annex V-B Block 13
Field Type
Physical state code(s)
Required For
All Basel movements

What Block 13 Captures

Block 13 declares the physical state of the waste under normal temperature and pressure conditions. It uses the same standardized code list as the notification document — the movement document must carry a consistent declaration. Competent authorities and emergency responders use this block during transit to understand the physical form of the material being carried.

For wastes with more than one physical state — such as lead-acid batteries, which have a solid casing and plates combined with a liquid electrolyte — all applicable codes must be declared. Declaring only one code when more apply is a common error that creates a misleading hazard profile for transport authorities.

Physical Characteristics Codes

1
Powdery / Powder — Fine solid particulate material.
2
Solid — Material with a defined shape and volume that does not flow under gravity.
3
Viscous / Paste — Semi-solid material that flows slowly under pressure.
4
Sludgy — A mixture of liquid and solid material with a semi-fluid consistency.
5
Liquid — Material that flows freely under gravity at normal temperature and pressure.
6
Gaseous — Material in gas phase at normal temperature and pressure.
7
Other — Any physical state not covered by codes 1–6. Must be described in full — do not select Other without specifying the state.
⚠️
Must Match the Approved Notification

The physical characteristics declared on the movement document must be consistent with what was declared on the notification. A discrepancy between the two documents will draw authority queries and can delay the shipment at the border.

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
Selecting only code 2 (Solid) for ULABs
Correct
Select both code 2 (Solid) and code 5 (Liquid) — ULABs contain solid plates and liquid sulfuric acid electrolyte
Wrong
Selecting code 7 (Other) without describing the physical state
Correct
Always provide a full description when selecting Other — never leave it unspecified
Wrong
Block 13 on the movement document differs from Block 13 on the approved notification
Correct
Both documents must carry identical physical characteristics codes — check consistency before dispatch
Wrong
No code selected — Block 13 left blank
Correct
At least one code must be declared — Block 13 is mandatory on every movement document

Frequently Asked Questions

Can more than one code be selected?▼

Yes. Where the waste has more than one physical state — as is the case with lead-acid batteries — all applicable codes should be declared. For ULABs, codes 2 (Solid) and 5 (Liquid) both apply.

Does Block 13 on the movement document need to match the notification exactly?▼

Yes. The movement document must be consistent with the approved notification. Any discrepancy in physical characteristics between the two documents can trigger authority queries at the border and delay the shipment.

What codes apply to sealed (VRLA/AGM) batteries that are non-spillable?▼

Sealed VRLA and AGM batteries still contain electrolyte in absorbed or gel form. Code 2 (Solid) applies to the casing and plates. Whether code 5 (Liquid) or code 3 (Viscous/Paste) applies to the electrolyte depends on the specific battery type — confirm with the battery manufacturer's technical data sheet and declare consistently with the approved notification.

Supporting Documents

  • vCOP8 Official Movement Document — Annex V-B Block 13 — Official Basel source for the physical characteristics code list and completion instructions.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

For ULAB exports, the correct Block 13 entry is codes 2 and 5 — Solid and Liquid. This applies to both flooded and sealed battery types. Declare it the same way on every movement document under a general notification to maintain consistency with the approved notification and avoid any document-to-document discrepancies that could attract scrutiny.

item.title: Block 4: Total Intended Number of Shipments
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 4: Total Intended Number of Shipments

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 4

Block 4 – Quick Reference

Total Intended Number of Shipments

Records the total count of individual shipments planned under this notification — the ceiling that movement documents cannot exceed.

Basel Basis
Article 6(1), Basel Convention; Annex V-A Block 4
Field Type
Numeric — whole number count of planned shipments
Required For
All Basel movements. Critical for general (multiple) notifications.

What Block 4 Captures

Block 4 records the maximum total number of individual shipments planned under this notification. This figure acts as a ceiling — authorities will not authorize more movement documents than the number declared here. For single notifications (Block 3 A(i)), this is always 1. For general notifications (Block 3 A(ii)), you must declare the total anticipated shipments for the entire validity period.

Authorities use Block 4 to set consent limits and to track whether actual movements stay within the approved scope. If you exceed the declared number without submitting a new notification, the movement becomes non-compliant.

How to Complete Block 4

1
Single notification (Block 3 A(i)). Enter 1. Single notifications cover exactly one shipment.
2
General notification (Block 3 A(ii)). Enter the maximum total number of individual shipments planned within the validity period. This is your ceiling — actual shipments cannot exceed this number.
3
Align with Block 5. Your shipment count should be realistic relative to the total intended quantity in Block 5. Divide total quantity by average shipment size to check consistency.
⚠️
Exceeding Block 4 Invalidates Consent

If actual shipments exceed the Block 4 total, you must submit a new notification and obtain fresh consent. Operating beyond the declared ceiling is a compliance breach.

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
Block 4 left blank on a general notification
Correct
Always specify the total — authorities use this to audit individual movement documents
Wrong
Entering 1 on a general notification when multiple shipments are planned
Correct
If multiple shipments are planned, the number must reflect the actual planned total
Wrong
Actual shipments exceed the Block 4 total
Correct
Submit a new notification before the declared ceiling is reached if more shipments are needed

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Block 4 always "1" for single notifications? ▼

Yes. A single notification (Block 3 A(i)) covers exactly one shipment, so Block 4 must be 1. Only general notifications (Block 3 A(ii)) can have a number greater than 1.

Can I exceed the Block 4 total later if I need more shipments? ▼

No. If you need more shipments than declared in Block 4, you must submit a new notification and obtain fresh consent from competent authorities. Operating beyond your declared ceiling is a compliance breach.

How does Block 4 relate to Block 5 (Total Intended Quantity)? ▼

Block 4 (quantity of shipments) and Block 5 (total quantity) should be consistent. Divide your total quantity by your planned number of shipments to ensure the average shipment size is realistic for your waste type and transport mode.

Supporting Documents

  • vCOP8 Official Form and Completion Instructions — Block 4 – Basel Convention official guidance on completing Block 4.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

For general notifications, build in headroom. If you plan 10 shipments, declare 12–14. Operational needs change — having unused capacity in Block 4 costs nothing, but running out mid-operation forces a resubmission and a full consent cycle.

item.title: Block 5: Total Intended Quantity
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 5: Total Intended Quantity

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 5

Block 5 – Quick Reference

Total Intended Quantity

Declares the total weight or volume of waste covered by this notification — the cumulative ceiling across all planned shipments.

Basel Basis
Article 6(1), Basel Convention; Annex V-A Block 5
Field Type
Quantity — weight in tonnes (Mg) or volume in m³
Required For
All Basel movements

What Block 5 Captures

Declares the total weight or volume of waste covered by this notification — the cumulative ceiling across all planned shipments. For general notifications (Block 3 A(ii)), this figure represents the maximum total across all individual movements. Individual movement documents must not cause the running total to exceed this declared ceiling.

How to Complete Block 5

1
Enter weight in tonnes (Mg). 1 tonne = 1,000 kg. This is the preferred unit.
2
If weight cannot be determined, enter volume in m³. 1 m³ = 1,000 litres.
3
If using kilograms or litres instead, cross out the printed unit on the form and write the actual unit used clearly.
4
For general notifications (Block 3 A(ii)): this figure is the maximum cumulative total across all planned shipments. Individual movement documents must not push the running total beyond this figure.
5
For general notifications, attach a schedule of expected individual shipment quantities as an annex.
⚠️
Cumulative Total Enforcement

Transit authorities verify that cumulative quantities across all movement documents do not exceed the Block 5 ceiling. Exceeding this total without amending the notification is a common violation.

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
Using kg without noting the unit change on the form
Correct
Cross out "Tonnes (Mg)" on the form and write "kg" clearly if using kilograms
Wrong
Underestimating total on a general notification
Correct
Cumulative total of all movement documents must not exceed Block 5 — budget generously
Wrong
Both tonnes and m³ left blank
Correct
At least one unit must be completed

Supporting Documents

  • vCOP8 Official Form and Completion Instructions — Block 5 – Official Basel Convention form and guidance for Block 5 completion.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

For general notifications, declare 15–20% more than your best quantity estimate. Operational volumes vary — exceeding the declared total forces a new notification mid-operation, causing shipment delays and additional authority processing time.

← Back to Block 4: Total Number of Shipments Next → Block 6: Intended Period of Time

item.title: Block 7: Packaging Type(s) & Special Handling
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 7: Packaging Type(s) & Special Handling

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 7

Block 7 – Quick Reference

Packaging Type(s) & Special Handling

Declares the packaging method(s) using standardized codes and flags any special handling requirements.

Basel Basis
Annex V-A Block 7; vCOP8 packaging code list
Field Type
Packaging codes + special handling Yes/No flag
Required For
All Basel movements

What Block 7 Captures

Block 7 declares the packaging method(s) used for the waste during transport. It uses standardized UN packaging codes and indicates whether special handling is required.

Multiple packaging codes may apply to a single shipment. Special handling flags requirements such as upright orientation, temperature control, or shock sensitivity.

Packaging Type Codes

Code Type
1Drum
2Wooden barrel
3Jerrican
4Box
5Bag
6Composite packaging
7Pressure receptacle
8Bulk
9Other (specify)

How to Complete Block 7

1
Select all applicable packaging codes. Multiple codes may apply to a single shipment.
2
Indicate special handling requirements. If special handling is required, tick Yes and attach details as a numbered annex. Special handling includes requirements such as upright orientation, temperature control, shock protection, or specific loading/unloading procedures.
3
Specify "Other" packaging. If code 9 (Other) is selected, describe the packaging type in full.
⚠️
ULAB Note

Standard packaging is code 8 (Bulk on pallets) or code 1 (Drum). Special handling Yes is appropriate where batteries containing electrolyte must be kept upright during transport and storage.

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
No packaging code selected
Correct
At least one packaging code must be declared
Wrong
Special handling No for ULABs requiring upright orientation
Correct
Tick Yes and attach handling instructions when electrolyte retention requires specific orientation
Wrong
Code 9 used without specifying packaging type
Correct
Always describe the packaging when selecting Other

Frequently Asked Questions

Can multiple packaging codes be declared for one shipment? ▼

Yes. Multiple packaging codes may apply to a single shipment. For example, a shipment might include some waste in drums (code 1) and some in boxes (code 4).

What constitutes "special handling"? ▼

Special handling includes any requirements such as upright orientation (to prevent electrolyte leakage), temperature control, shock protection, or specific loading/unloading procedures. These must be documented and attached as a numbered annex.

When should code 9 (Other) be used? ▼

Code 9 should only be used when the packaging type does not fit any of the standard codes 1-8. When using code 9, you must fully describe the packaging type in the designated field.

Supporting Documents

  • vCOP8 Official Form and Completion Instructions — Block 7 – Official Basel Convention form and guidance for completing Block 7.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

Special handling annexes attached under Block 7 should include producer handling instructions, health and safety data sheets, spill response procedures, and transport emergency cards where required by the importing country's legislation.

item.title: Block 8: Intended Carrier(s)
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 8: Intended Carrier(s)

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 8

Block 8 – Quick Reference

Intended Carrier(s)

Identifies the carrier or carriers who will physically transport the waste and the means of transport.

Basel Basis
Article 6(1), Basel Convention; Annex V-A Block 8
Field Type
Party identity — carrier(s) and transport mode codes
Required For
All Basel movements

What Block 8 Captures

Block 8 identifies who will carry the waste and how. For sea freight this typically means the shipping line or freight forwarder. If a forwarding agent organizes the transport but does not carry the waste themselves, the agent's details go in Block 8 and the actual carriers are listed in an attached annex.

Means of Transport Codes

Code Mode
RRoad
TTrain / Rail
SSea
AAir
WInland waterways

How to Complete Block 8

1
Enter the carrier's registration or licence number, full legal name, full address (including country), contact person, telephone, fax, and email.
2
Enter the means of transport code. Use multiple codes if the shipment uses more than one mode (e.g., R + S for road to port then sea freight).
3
If more than one carrier is involved, append a complete carrier list as a numbered annex. Write "See attached list" in Block 8.
4
If a forwarding agent organizes the transport, enter the agent's details here and list actual carriers in an annex.
⚠️
Forwarding Agent vs. Actual Carrier

If a forwarding agent organizes the transport but does not carry the waste themselves, the agent's details go in Block 8 and the actual carriers must be listed in an attached annex.

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
Means of transport code omitted
Correct
Always declare the transport mode — it is mandatory
Wrong
Forwarding agent listed but actual carriers not attached as annex
Correct
Attach a full carrier annex whenever an agent organizes transport
Wrong
Carrier details on notification differ from movement document
Correct
Both documents must carry consistent carrier information
Wrong
Only S (Sea) listed when road transport is used to reach the port
Correct
List all modes used — R + S if road is used for the domestic leg to port

Frequently Asked Questions

What if the final carrier is not known at notification stage? ▼

Provide the best available information — typically the freight forwarder or shipping agent. The movement document (completed at shipment time) captures the actual carrier with signatures.

Does the carrier need to be registered with any authority? ▼

Many countries require carriers of hazardous waste to hold a specific transport licence. Include the licence number in the registration field where applicable.

Who completes Block 8? ▼

Block 8 is completed by the exporter/notifier when preparing the notification. The carrier details should be confirmed before submission.

Supporting Documents

  • vCOP8 Official Form and Completion Instructions — Block 8 — Official Basel Convention form and instructions for Block 8 completion.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

For ULAB sea freight from T&T, declare R + S as transport modes. The domestic leg to Port of Spain or Point Lisas uses road; the international leg uses sea. Declaring only S will draw queries from customs and transport authorities.

← Back to Block 7: Packaging Type(s) Next → Block 9: Waste Generator-Producer

item.title: Block 9: Waste Generator-Producer
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 9: Waste Generator-Producer

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 9

Block 9 – Quick Reference

Waste Generator(s)-Producer(s)

Identifies the entity that generated the waste, the site of generation, and the process by which it was produced.

Basel Basis
Article 2(19), Article 6(1), Basel Convention; Annex V-A Block 9
Field Type
Party identity — waste generator(s) and generation process
Required For
Required by Basel Convention. Not required under OECD Decision for recovery movements — but most authorities expect it.

What Block 9 Captures

Block 9 establishes the origin of the waste — who produced it, where, and through what process. The Basel Convention requires this information for all transboundary movements to enable traceability from source to final treatment. Where the true generator is unknown, Article 2(19) of the Basel Convention deems the person in possession or control of the waste to be the generator.

How to Complete Block 9

1
If the exporter (Block 1) is also the generator, write "Same as Block 1" and complete the site and process of generation fields below.
2
If the exporter is not the generator, enter the generator's registration number (where applicable), full legal name, address, and contact details.
3
Describe the site of generation — the specific location where the waste was produced or collected.
4
Describe the process of generation — how the waste came into existence (e.g., Collection and aggregation of end-of-life lead-acid batteries from automotive workshops, retail battery outlets, and industrial users across Trinidad and Tobago).
5
If more than one generator is involved, write "See attached list" and append full details for each in a numbered annex.

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
Block 9 left blank because OECD Decision does not require it
Correct
Basel Convention requires it — include for all movements regardless of instrument
Wrong
"Unknown" entered as generator name
Correct
Where the true generator is unknown, the person in possession or control is deemed the generator — use their details
Wrong
Vague process description: "collection of batteries"
Correct
Be specific — name the types, sources, and geographic scope of collection
Wrong
Generator details left off when exporter and generator differ
Correct
Both entities must be identified separately — exporter in Block 1, generator in Block 9
Wrong
Multiple generators listed inline without an annex
Correct
Use "See attached list" and provide full details for each generator in a numbered annex

Frequently Asked Questions

If I collected batteries from many sources, who is the generator? ▼

The collector/aggregator is the generator for Basel purposes where the original producers cannot be individually identified. Use your own entity details and describe the collection process in the site/process field.

Does the generator need to sign the notification? ▼

The generator is required to sign Block 17 (the declaration) where practicable. Where it is not practicable (e.g., multiple anonymous sources), document the reason.

Can generator details be kept confidential? ▼

Some countries permit generator details to be submitted in a confidential annex available only to competent authorities. Check the importing country's requirements.

Supporting Documents

  • vCOP8 Official Form and Completion Instructions — Block 9 – Official Basel Convention form and instructions for completing Block 9.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

A well-written site and process description in Block 9 reduces the likelihood of authority queries about waste origin. For ULAB exporters, describe the collection network, the battery types accepted, and the geographic area covered — even one paragraph is significantly better than a blank field.

← Back to Block 8: Intended Carrier(s) Next → Block 10: Disposal/Recovery Facility

item.title: Block 10: Disposal/Recovery Facility
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 10: Disposal/Recovery Facility

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 10

Block 10 – Quick Reference

Disposal/Recovery Facility

Identifies the authorized facility that will receive and process the waste under this notification.

Basel Basis
Annex V-A Block 10; ESM principles
Field Type
Party identity — destination facility
Required For
All Basel movements

What Block 10 Captures

Block 10 establishes the legal identity of the receiving facility — the specific authorized site where the waste will be disposed of or recovered. Competent authorities use this block to verify that the declared destination holds a valid permit for the declared waste type and operation. The facility declared here must remain valid for the entire consent period — not just at the time of notification.

Block 10 identifies where the waste is going. What happens to it there is declared in Block 11.

How to Complete Block 10

1
Tick either Disposal Facility or Recovery Facility. These are not interchangeable and must match Block 3 (B(i) or B(ii)) and Block 11.
2
Enter the facility's registration or permit number as issued by the competent authority in the country of import.
3
Enter the exact legal name as it appears on the facility's authorization. Do not use trading names or abbreviations.
4
Enter the full address. If the actual processing site differs from the registered address, enter the registered address here and complete the Actual site of disposal/recovery sub-field.
5
If the disposer or recoverer is also the importer (Block 2), write "Same as Block 2".
⚠️
Interim Operations (R12/R13, D13–D15)

If the declared operation in Block 11 is an interim code, attach an annex identifying all subsequent facilities and the final operation code where actual processing is completed.

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
Trading name instead of legal name on permit
Correct
Use exact name from the facility authorization document
Wrong
Registration number omitted
Correct
Always include where one exists — omission delays consent
Wrong
Actual processing site differs from address but sub-field left blank
Correct
Complete the actual site sub-field whenever the physical location differs from the registered address
Wrong
Facility permit expires during the notification period
Correct
Verify permit currency before each individual shipment, not just at notification stage

Frequently Asked Questions

Can the facility change after the notification is approved? ▼

Only through a formal variation process managed by the competent authority. Routing waste to a different facility without prior approval is a critical compliance breach.

What if the facility is also the importer? ▼

Write "Same as Block 2" in Block 10. No need to repeat all contact details.

Supporting Documents

  • vCOP8 Official Form and Completion Instructions — Block 10 – Official Basel Convention form and completion guidance.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

Request a copy of the facility's current permit before submitting. Attaching it as an annex proactively answers the most common authority query about Block 10 and can materially speed up consent turnaround.

item.title: Block 11: Disposal/Recovery Operation
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 11: Disposal/Recovery Operation

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 11

Block 11 – Quick Reference

Disposal/Recovery Operation

Declares the approved R or D operation code, the technology employed, and the reason for export.

Basel Basis
Annex IV-A/B, Basel Convention
Field Type
Operation code (R/D), technology, reason
Required For
All Basel movements

What Block 11 Captures

Block 11 declares what will actually happen to the waste at the receiving facility. It contains three sub-fields: the R or D operation code, the technology employed, and the reason for export. Competent authorities use Block 11 together with Block 10 (facility identity) to verify that the declared operation matches the facility's permit scope and that the technology described is environmentally sound.

If Block 10 tells authorities where the waste is going, Block 11 tells them what happens to it. A mismatch between these two blocks is one of the most common causes of notification rejection.

R-Codes: Recovery Operations

Code Operation
R1Use as fuel or other energy generation
R2Solvent reclamation/regeneration
R3Recycling/reclamation of organic substances (non-solvent)
R4Recycling/reclamation of metals and metal compounds
R5Recycling/reclamation of other inorganic materials
R6Regeneration of acids or bases
R7Recovery of components for pollution abatement
R8Recovery of components from catalysts
R9Used oil re-refining or other reuses of previously used oil
R10Land treatment for agricultural or ecological benefit
R11Uses of residual materials from R1–R10
R12Exchange of wastes for submission to R1–R11 (interim only)
R13Accumulation of material intended for any operation in this list (interim only)
⚠️
ULAB Note

Lead-acid battery recycling for lead recovery uses R4 (metals and metal compounds). Confirm against the receiving facility's authorization before declaring.

D-Codes: Disposal Operations

Code Operation
D1Deposit into or onto land (landfill)
D2Land treatment (biodegradation)
D3Deep injection
D4Surface impoundment
D5Specially engineered landfill
D6Release into water body (except seas/oceans)
D7Release into seas/oceans
D8Biological treatment not elsewhere specified
D9Physico-chemical treatment not elsewhere specified
D10Incineration on land
D11Incineration at sea
D12Permanent storage
D13Blending or mixing prior to another D operation (interim only)
D14Repackaging prior to another D operation (interim only)
D15Storage pending any D operation (interim only)

How to Complete Block 11

1
Confirm the operation type. Determine whether the movement is for disposal or recovery. This must match Block 3 (B(i) or B(ii)).
2
Select the operation code. Choose the single most accurate R or D code. Do not list multiple codes unless the waste genuinely undergoes multiple operations.
3
Describe the technology. Specify the actual process used at the facility. "Recycling" alone is not sufficient. Examples: pyrometallurgical smelting for lead recovery, hydrometallurgical leaching and electrowinning.
4
State the reason for export. Required by the Basel Convention. Examples: No certified lead smelting capacity exists in the country of export, No domestic facility holds authorization for this waste type.
5
Verify against facility permit. Cross-reference with Block 10 to confirm the declared operation is within the facility's authorized scope.
⚠️
R12/R13 and D13–D15 Interim Operations

If the declared operation is an interim code (R12, R13, D13, D14, or D15), you must attach an annex identifying all subsequent facilities and the final R1–R11 or D1–D12 operation where processing is completed.

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
Technology field left blank or states only "recycling"
Correct
Specify the actual process — e.g., pyrometallurgical smelting, hydrometallurgical processing
Wrong
Reason for export left blank
Correct
Required by Basel Convention — state the specific reason domestic treatment is not used
Wrong
R and D codes used interchangeably
Correct
Recovery (R) and disposal (D) are legally distinct categories — use the correct one
Wrong
R13 declared as final operation
Correct
R13 is interim only — attach annex naming the subsequent R1–R11 facility
Wrong
Code does not match facility permit scope in Block 10
Correct
Verify the facility is authorized for the exact declared operation before submitting

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I change the operation code after consent is granted? ▼

No. Any change to the declared operation requires a formal variation through the competent authority before the shipment departs. Changing codes on the movement document without authority approval is a compliance breach.

What if my waste goes through an interim operation before final recovery? ▼

Declare the interim operation (e.g., R13 for accumulation) in Block 11 and attach an annex identifying the subsequent facility where the final operation (e.g., R4) takes place.

Is the reason for export required for all movements? ▼

Required by the Basel Convention. The OECD Decision does not require it, but most competent authorities — including in OECD countries — expect it. Always include it.

What is the difference between Block 10 and Block 11? ▼

Block 10 identifies the facility — who and where. Block 11 declares the operation — what happens to the waste. Both must be consistent with each other and with the approved consent.

Supporting Documents

  • vCOP8 Official Form and Completion Instructions — Block 11 — Official Basel source for R/D code definitions and completion rules.
  • Basel Convention Annexes IV-A and IV-B — Complete disposal and recovery operation code lists.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

Block 11 is consistently cited as a top cause of notification rejection. Vague technology descriptions and missing reason-for-export text are the two most frequent triggers. Write both as complete sentences before submitting.

item.title: Block 12: Designation & Composition of the Waste
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 12: Designation & Composition of the Waste

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 12

Block 12 – Quick Reference

Designation & Composition of the Waste

Describes the waste by its common name and lists major constituents with approximate concentrations.

Basel Basis
Article 4(2)(d), Basel Convention; Annex V-A Block 12
Field Type
Descriptive — commercial/common name and constituent composition
Required For
All Basel movements

What Block 12 Captures

Block 12 describes what the waste actually is in both plain and technical terms. It requires the common or commercial name of the waste and a breakdown of its major constituents with their approximate concentrations. Competent authorities use this block to cross-check the waste description against the classification codes in Block 14 and to assess environmental and health risks during transit.

For mixed wastes, each distinct fraction must be described separately, with its intended operation noted. A chemical analysis may be required under the national legislation of the importing or transit country — attach as an annex if so.

How to Complete Block 12

1
Enter the common or commercial name by which the waste is known (e.g., Used Lead-Acid Batteries, Spent ULAB — flooded and VRLA types).
2
List the major constituents by name with approximate percentage concentrations by weight. Ranges are acceptable where exact values are not known.
3
For mixed wastes, describe each fraction separately and indicate which fraction is destined for recovery and which for disposal.
4
If a chemical analysis is required by the importing country, attach it as an annex and reference it here.
⚠️
ULAB Example Entry

Common name: Used Lead-Acid Batteries (flooded and sealed VRLA/AGM types)
Major constituents: Lead and lead compounds ~60%, Polypropylene casing ~20%, Sulfuric acid electrolyte ~15%, Other (separators, copper terminals) ~5%

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
Generic description: "hazardous waste" or "battery scrap"
Correct
Use the specific commercial name and list all major constituents
Wrong
No constituent percentages given
Correct
Approximate concentrations are required — ranges are acceptable
Wrong
Mixture fractions not separately described
Correct
Each distinct fraction must be identified with its own name, composition, and intended operation
Wrong
Composition inconsistent with Block 14 waste codes
Correct
The description in Block 12 must logically support the classification codes declared in Block 14
Wrong
Chemical analysis required by importing country not attached
Correct
Check importing country requirements — attach analysis as a numbered annex and reference it in Block 18

Frequently Asked Questions

Does "approximate" mean I can round figures broadly?▼

Approximate percentages should be as accurate as reasonably possible. Competent authorities use these figures to assess risk — figures like "Lead: 10–90%" are too broad to be useful and will trigger queries.

Is a formal laboratory analysis always required?▼

Not universally — but many importing countries require it by national law. Check the competent authority requirements for the specific country of import before submission.

What if the composition varies across batches?▼

Provide the typical range for each constituent and note that composition is representative. For materials like ULABs with consistent chemistry, this is straightforward.

Supporting Documents

  • vCOP8 Official Form and Completion Instructions — Block 12 — Official Basel Convention form instructions for Block 12 completion.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

Block 12 and Block 14 must tell a consistent story. If Block 12 describes lead-acid batteries, Block 14 should carry code A1160 and Y-code Y31. Authorities cross-check these fields — inconsistencies are a primary rejection trigger.

Next →Block 13: Physical Characteristics

item.title: Block 13: Waste Physical Characteristics
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 13: Waste Physical Characteristics

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 13

Block 13 — Quick Reference

Waste Physical Characteristics

Describes the observable physical state of the waste at time of shipment — form, colour, odour, and specific gravity.

Basel Article
Annex V A, Item 13
Rejection Risk
Low — Descriptive field
Cross-references
Block 12, Block 16

What Block 13 Captures

Block 13 records the observable physical properties of the waste as it exists at time of handover to the carrier. The primary fields are physical state (solid, liquid, sludge, gas, or mixed), colour, odour, and specific gravity or density. This description serves as a baseline against which the receiving facility can verify the shipment arrived in expected condition. For ULAB specifically, the typical description is: Solid — Used lead-acid batteries in various states of discharge. Grey/black exterior casings, electrolyte contained. Slight sulphurous odour. Specific gravity: approx. 1.28 SG (electrolyte). Significant deviations from this at reception indicate either misidentification of waste or leakage during transit.

How to Complete Block 13

1
Select physical state. For ULAB: Solid. For battery acid or electrolyte waste: Liquid. For mixed loads containing both batteries and acid: Mixed. If unsure, describe as Solid unless liquid content exceeds 10% by volume.
2
Describe colour and appearance. Be accurate and specific. “Grey polypropylene cases with lead terminals” is better than “grey.” A description that matches the actual waste helps inspectors clear the shipment faster.
3
Note odour if significant. ULAB have a mild sulphurous odour from sulphuric acid electrolyte. Cracked or damaged batteries will have a stronger odour. Note whether odour is faint, moderate, or strong to assist facility receiving staff.
4
Enter specific gravity if known. For lead-acid battery electrolyte: 1.26–1.30 SG depending on state of charge. For the solid battery units themselves, this field is often left blank or noted as N/A. Check with your facility’s analytical data if available.
✅
Lower Rejection Risk — But Accuracy Still Matters

Block 13 is rarely the sole cause of rejection, but inaccurate physical descriptions create problems at the port of arrival. If the actual shipment doesn’t match the described characteristics, customs can hold or reject the consignment pending investigation.

Common Errors → Correct Approach

❌ Wrong
Describing a mixed battery/electrolyte load as “Solid” when significant liquid content is present
✅ Correct
Describe as “Mixed” and quantify approximate liquid percentage — e.g., “Predominantly solid with approx. 5% residual electrolyte by volume”
❌ Wrong
Leaving colour/appearance blank because it seems obvious
✅ Correct
Complete all fields — “Grey and black polypropylene battery casings, lead terminals, electrolyte contained” takes 10 seconds and prevents customs queries

Frequently Asked Questions

What physical state should I declare for cracked or leaking ULAB?▼
Cracked or leaking ULAB should be classified as Mixed, not Solid, since liquid electrolyte is escaping the casing. This also triggers stricter packaging requirements — the outer container must be capable of retaining the electrolyte. Declaring cracked batteries as Solid when they are actively leaking is a misrepresentation of the waste.
Is an analytical report required to complete Block 13?▼
Not mandatory for Block 13 itself. An analytical report is typically required for Block 16 (composition) and supporting documentation. Block 13 accepts visual/operational descriptions. However, if a competent authority requests verification, an analytical report or laboratory assessment of physical properties may be required.

Supporting Documents

  • Official Form Instructions (Physical characteristics codes) - Official Annex V-A/V-B forms and completion instructions.
  • OECD Movement Document Code Tables - OECD decision text and movement/operation code instructions.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

Take photographs of a representative sample of the waste at time of packing. Store these with your notification records. If physical characteristics are challenged at arrival, photos dated at point of origin are your strongest evidence that the waste matched the declared description when it left your facility.

item.title: Block 14: Waste Identification and Classification
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 14: Waste Identification and Classification

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 14

Block 14 — Quick Reference

Waste Identification and Classification

Assigns Basel Y-codes, A/B-codes, H hazard codes, UN numbers, and customs HS codes to formally classify the waste under international law.

Basel Article
Annexes I, II, VIII, IX
Rejection Risk
Critical — Wrong codes = illegal traffic
ULAB Code
Y31 / A1181 / H6, H8

What Block 14 Captures

Block 14 is the legal classification of your waste under the Basel Convention. It assigns four distinct code types: the Y-code (Annex I category), the A or B-code (Annex VIII/IX list), the H hazard characteristic code, and the UN transport number. Optionally, the customs HS code is also recorded here for border clearance purposes. This block determines whether the waste is subject to the full prior informed consent (PIC) procedure, the simplified procedure, or whether it is classified as non-hazardous. An incorrect classification in Block 14 does not just result in rejection — it can constitute illegal traffic under Article 9 of the Basel Convention, with criminal liability in some jurisdictions.

ULAB Reference Codes — Block 14

Code Type Code Description
Y-code Y31 Lead-acid batteries — used/scrap
A-code A1181 Waste lead-acid batteries, whole or crushed (Annex VIII — hazardous)
H-code H6.1, H8 H6.1: Toxic substances; H8: Corrosives (sulphuric acid)
UN Number UN 2794 Batteries, wet, filled with acid (for intact ULAB)
HS Code 8548.10 Waste and scrap of primary cells, primary batteries, and electric accumulators (customs)

How to Complete Block 14

1
Enter Y-code(s). For ULAB: Y31. If the waste includes other battery types (nickel-cadmium, lithium), add their Y-codes as well. Multiple Y-codes are permitted. See E-Waste Classifications for codes beyond ULAB.
2
Enter Annex VIII or IX code. For ULAB: A1181 (Annex VIII — confirms hazardous classification). Check Annex IX (B-codes) only if claiming non-hazardous status for a specific fraction. Most ULAB export requires A1181, not a B-code.
3
Enter H hazard code(s). For ULAB: H6.1 (toxic, for lead content) and H8 (corrosive, for sulphuric acid electrolyte). Both codes typically apply. Some notifiers also add H13 (capable of yielding hazardous substances after disposal) depending on CA requirements in the destination country.
4
Enter UN transport number. For intact ULAB: UN 2794. For crushed/processed batteries: UN 2800 (batteries, wet, non-spillable) or confirm with your dangerous goods consultant. The UN number governs transport documentation, not just the Basel form.
5
Enter HS code (customs field). Use 8548.10 for scrap batteries. This code is used by customs authorities for tariff classification. Some countries have export licensing requirements tied to this HS code — verify with your freight forwarder before finalising.
🚫
Wrong Classification = Illegal Traffic

Under Article 9 of the Basel Convention, waste transported with incorrect or falsified classification constitutes illegal traffic. This exposes the exporter, carrier, and receiving facility to criminal liability. If you are unsure which codes apply to a mixed waste stream, seek qualified legal or technical advice before submitting the notification.

Common Errors → Correct Approach

❌ Wrong
Using B1160 (Annex IX) to claim non-hazardous status for mixed ULAB loads without confirmation of B1160 eligibility
✅ Correct
ULAB for recovery require A1181 (Annex VIII). B1160 applies only to cleaned, drained, and otherwise processed battery fractions — not whole used batteries
❌ Wrong
Declaring H8 only and omitting H6.1 — underreporting hazard characteristics to avoid routing restrictions
✅ Correct
Declare all applicable H-codes. For ULAB: H6.1 and H8 both apply. Omitting a hazard code is misrepresentation under the Convention.
❌ Wrong
Using Y49 (e-waste category) for lead-acid batteries because it seems broader
✅ Correct
Use Y31 for lead-acid batteries specifically. Y49 applies to e-waste equipment. Using the wrong Y-code causes classification mismatches that trigger CA queries.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between A1181 and B1160 for battery waste?▼
A1181 (Annex VIII) classifies waste lead-acid batteries as hazardous, triggering the full PIC procedure. B1160 (Annex IX) classifies used batteries destined for direct re-use as non-hazardous, subject only to the Article 11 bilateral agreement procedure. For whole ULAB destined for smelting or recycling — not re-use — A1181 is the correct classification. Using B1160 for recycling-bound ULAB is a misclassification.
Does the Basel Ban Amendment affect which codes I use?▼
The Basel Ban Amendment (Decision III/1) prohibits hazardous waste exports from Annex VII countries (OECD, EU, Liechtenstein) to non-Annex VII countries for disposal. Codes alone do not change — but the Ban Amendment determines whether your movement is legally permissible at all, regardless of correct coding. If exporting from an OECD country to a non-OECD country, verify Ban Amendment applicability before filing.
Can I use the same Block 14 codes for all battery types?▼
No. Each battery chemistry has specific codes. Lead-acid: Y31/A1181. Nickel-cadmium: Y26/A1020. Lithium: covered under Y31 for used batteries but may also require Y36 (organics) depending on composition. Mixed battery loads require multiple Y-codes and the applicable A-codes for each type present in the shipment.

Supporting Documents

  • Basel Annex VIII – List A - Basel Annex VIII (List A) hazardous waste entries.
  • Basel Annex IX – List B - Basel Annex IX (List B) non-hazardous entries.
  • Basel Waste Identification Tool - Waste identification decision tool for Basel classification.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

Block 14 is the block most frequently scrutinised by competent authorities. Before submission, cross-reference your codes against the Basel Convention Annexes directly at basel.int. A second set of eyes from a qualified Basel consultant on Block 14 alone is worth the cost for first-time notifiers.

item.title: Block 15: Countries/States Concerned & Border Crossings
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 15: Countries/States Concerned & Border Crossings

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 15

Block 15 – Quick Reference

Countries/States Concerned & Border Crossing Points

Maps the complete geographic route of the movement from State of export through all transit States to the State of import.

Basel Basis
Article 6(1), Basel Convention; Annex V-A Block 15
Field Type
Country identification + competent authority codes + border crossing points
Required For
All Basel movements

What Block 15 Captures

Block 15 maps every country the waste will pass through from departure to final destination. For each country, three lines of information are required: the country name or ISO code, the competent authority code where required, and the specific border crossing or port of entry and exit. Missing transit countries is one of the most serious errors possible — a shipment passing through an undeclared transit state without prior consent is an illegal transboundary movement under the Basel Convention.

The Three Lines Per Country

Line (a) — Country name / ISO code: Use ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes. Examples: TT = Trinidad and Tobago, NL = Netherlands, DE = Germany, BE = Belgium.

Line (b) — Competent authority code: The code number of the competent authority in each country, where required by that country's national legislation. Check the Basel Convention country profiles for each State.

Line (c) — Border crossing or port: The specific point of exit from each country and point of entry into the next. For sea movements, this is the port of loading and port of discharge. For transit countries, give both entry and exit points.

How to Complete Block 15

1
Enter State of export (column 1): ISO code, CA code if required, and port or border crossing of exit.
2
Enter each State of transit (middle columns): ISO code, CA code, and both the entry and exit crossing points.
3
Enter State of import (final column): ISO code, CA code if required, and port or border crossing of entry.
4
If more than three transit countries are involved, attach additional country information as a numbered annex.
⚠️
Transit Consent Required

Under the Basel Convention, each transit State must provide written consent to the movement unless it has formally notified the Basel Secretariat that it does not require such consent. Omitting a transit country means no consent has been obtained — the movement is illegal in that jurisdiction.

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
Transit countries omitted
Correct
Every transit state must be declared — failure to do so constitutes illegal movement through that country
Wrong
Country name written without ISO code
Correct
Use ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes as required by vCOP8
Wrong
Port name given without specific terminal or customs point
Correct
Be as specific as possible — name the port and where applicable the specific terminal or customs entry point
Wrong
More than three transit countries without an annex
Correct
Attach a numbered annex for any transit countries beyond the three columns on the form
Wrong
Transshipment port listed as transit State when cargo is not offloaded
Correct
Transshipment at sea without offloading generally does not constitute transit — confirm with the shipping route and relevant authorities

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the ISO code for Trinidad and Tobago? ▼

TT. The port of export will typically be Port of Port of Spain or Point Lisas Industrial Port (La Brea).

Does a ship passing through a canal count as transit? ▼

Passage through an international waterway such as the Panama Canal or Suez Canal is not generally treated as transit through that State for Basel purposes — but confirm with the relevant competent authorities for your specific route.

How do I find competent authority codes for each country? ▼

The Basel Convention Secretariat maintains a directory of competent authorities at basel.int. DexMetal's Basel API also provides verified competent authority contact data for 41 countries.

Supporting Documents

  • vCOP8 Official Form and Completion Instructions — Block 15 – Official form and instructions from the Basel Convention.
  • DexMetal Basel API – Verified competent authority contact data for 41 countries.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

Confirm your full shipping route — including all intermediate ports where cargo may be offloaded — before completing Block 15. A route change after consent is granted requires notification to all competent authorities. Build route certainty into your logistics planning before submitting.

item.title: Block 16: Customs Offices (EU Member States Only)
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 16: Customs Offices (EU Member States Only)

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 16

Block 16 – Quick Reference

Customs Offices (EU Member States Only)

Records the specific EU customs offices of entry, exit, and export. Only required for movements entering, transiting, or leaving EU member states.

Basel Basis
EU Regulation 1013/2006; Annex V-A Block 16
Field Type
Customs office identification — EU movements only
Required For
Movements involving EU member states only

What Block 16 Captures

Block 16 is an EU-specific field that records the customs office codes at points where the waste enters, transits, or exits EU territory. It does not apply to movements wholly outside the EU. For exporters in non-EU countries shipping to non-EU destinations, this block is left blank.

How to Complete Block 16

If your movement does not involve any EU member state: Leave Block 16 blank entirely.

If your movement involves the EU:

1
Entry — Enter the customs office code where the waste enters EU territory.
2
Exit — Enter the customs office code where the waste leaves EU territory.
3
Export — Enter the customs office code where EU export formalities are completed. Use official EU customs office codes — port or city names alone are not sufficient.

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
Completing Block 16 for a non-EU movement
Correct
Leave blank — this field only applies to movements involving EU member states
Wrong
Writing a port or city name instead of a customs office code
Correct
Use official EU customs office identification codes
Wrong
Confusing Block 16 (EU customs offices) with Block 15 (border crossings)
Correct
Block 15 covers all countries and border points; Block 16 is specifically for EU customs office codes

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Block 16 apply to ULAB exports from Trinidad and Tobago to the EU? ▼

Yes — if the destination country is an EU member state (e.g., Germany, Belgium, Netherlands), Block 16 must be completed with the relevant EU customs office codes at the port of entry.

Where do I find EU customs office codes? ▼

EU customs office codes are available through the EU's TARIC database and from the customs authority of the relevant EU member state.

Supporting Documents

  • vCOP8 Official Form and Completion Instructions — Block 16 – Official form and instructions for completing Block 16.
  • EU Customs Office Reference Data (TARIC) – Official EU database for customs office codes.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

For most T&T ULAB exporters shipping to non-EU destinations, Block 16 is simply left blank. If your destination is within the EU, contact the receiving facility or your freight forwarder for the correct customs office codes — they handle EU customs formalities routinely and will have this information.

item.title: Block 17: Exporter & Generator Declaration
item.dc:creator: rdavid@gvoltt.com
item.content:encoded:
Block 17: Exporter & Generator Declaration

← Basel Knowledge Hub / Basel Form Guide / Block 17

Block 17 – Quick Reference

Exporter & Generator Declaration

The legal declaration that the notification is complete, accurate, and that contractual obligations and financial guarantees are in place.

Basel Basis
Article 6(1), Basel Convention; Annex V-A Block 17
Field Type
Legal declaration — signatures and certification
Required For
All Basel movements

What Block 17 Captures

Block 17 is the legal declaration that certifies three things: (1) all information in the notification is complete and correct to the best of the notifier's knowledge; (2) legally enforceable written contractual obligations have been entered into between all parties; and (3) applicable insurance or other financial guarantee is or will be in force covering the transboundary movement.

This block must be signed last — after all other blocks are complete. Signing before completing the form undermines the certification and can create legal liability if errors are subsequently found.

How to Complete Block 17

1
Ensure every other block in the notification is complete and reviewed before signing.
2
Confirm that a written contract between the exporter, importer, and facility is in place or will be in place before the shipment departs.
3
Confirm that insurance or a financial guarantee covering the movement is in place or arranged.
4
Enter the exporter/notifier's printed name, sign, and date in DD.MM.YY format.
5
Obtain the waste generator's printed name, signature, and date where practicable. If impracticable (e.g., multiple unknown generators), document the reason.
⚠️
Electronic Submissions

A digital signature is required for electronically submitted notifications. Check the importing country's accepted digital signature standards before submission.

Common Errors – Correct Approach

Wrong
Generator signature omitted without documented reason
Correct
Basel Convention requires generator signature where practicable — record the reason if genuinely impracticable
Wrong
Signing before all other blocks are complete
Correct
Block 17 certifies the entire form — always sign last
Wrong
No contract or insurance in place at time of signing
Correct
The declaration certifies these exist or will be in force — do not sign if they have not been arranged
Wrong
Date written in wrong format
Correct
Use DD.MM.YY — e.g., 21.02.26 for 21 February 2026

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a stamped signature required or will a printed name suffice? ▼

A handwritten signature is required for paper submissions. Some countries additionally require a company stamp. Check the importing country's specific requirements.

Does the financial guarantee need to be submitted with the notification? ▼

Some countries require proof of insurance or guarantee to accompany the notification. Others accept the declaration alone. Check importing country requirements.

What constitutes a "legally enforceable written contractual obligation"? ▼

A signed contract between the exporter, importer, and receiving facility that governs the terms of the waste transfer, processing, and liability. This should be in place — or at minimum agreed in principle — before Block 17 is signed.

Supporting Documents

  • vCOP8 Official Form and Completion Instructions — Block 17 – Official Basel Convention documentation.
💡
DexMetal Expert Tip

Treat Block 17 as your quality gate. Before signing, run through the entire notification one final time. Competent authorities cannot unsee errors once a signed notification is in their hands — a well-reviewed form submitted once is faster than a corrected resubmission.
